subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Energy cycles in reactions
bigPicture: Enthalpy depends only on where a reaction starts and finishes, not on the route. That single idea (Hess's law) lets us calculate enthalpy changes we cannot measure, using bond enthalpies, enthalpies of formation or combustion, or a Born–Haber cycle for ionic compounds.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you calculate ΔH from bond enthalpies?
keyIdeas.answer: Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases it. ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed), all species gaseous. Bond enthalpies in the booklet are averages over many compounds, so the answer is approximate, and it is wrong if any substance is not a gas.

keyIdeas.cue: What is Hess's law and how do you use it?
keyIdeas.answer: The total enthalpy change is independent of the pathway. Build a cycle or add equations: reverse an equation → change the sign of ΔH; multiply an equation → multiply ΔH.

ΔHf⦵: enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states (elements = 0). ΔHc⦵: enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen. Be able to write the matching equations, e.g. formation of ethanol: 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l).

keyIdeas.cue: Which equations use ΔHf and ΔHc data (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants). ΔH = Σ ΔHc(reactants) − Σ ΔHc(products). Multiply each value by its coefficient. Both are in the data booklet.

A Hess cycle for an ionic solid: atomise the metal and the non-metal, ionise the metal (IE), add electrons to the non-metal (EA), then bring the gaseous ions together (−lattice enthalpy). The steps add up to ΔHf. Use it to find an unknown value, such as lattice enthalpy, for compounds with 1+/2+ and 1−/2− ions. You won't be asked to construct a full cycle from scratch.

keyTerms.def: Energy to break one mole of a given bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over many compounds.
ΔH for a reaction is independent of the route.
ΔH when 1 mol of compound forms from its elements in standard states (AHL).
ΔH when 1 mol of substance burns completely in O₂ (AHL).
Enthalpy to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions (endothermic) (AHL).
ΔH to form 1 mol of gaseous atoms from the element (AHL).

workedExamples.title: Bond enthalpies
workedExamples.prompt: Estimate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) (C–H 414, O=O 498, C=O 804, O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹).
workedExamples.answer: −808 kJ mol⁻¹ (less exothermic than ΔHc = −891 because water is a gas here and values are averages)

workedExamples.title: From ΔHf data (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: Calculate ΔHc of ethanol using ΔHf: C₂H₅OH(l) −278, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286 kJ mol⁻¹.

workedExamples.title: Born–Haber (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: Find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl from: ΔHf(NaCl) −411; atomisation Na +107; ½ Cl–Cl bond +121; IE(Na) +496; EA(Cl) −349 kJ mol⁻¹.

misconceptions.right: It is broken − formed (energy in minus energy out).

misconceptions.wrong: The ΔHf of O₂(g) is −249 kJ mol⁻¹.
misconceptions.right: Elements in their standard states have ΔHf = 0 by definition.

misconceptions.wrong: ΔHc data use the same 'products − reactants' rule as ΔHf data.
misconceptions.right: Order matters: ΔHf uses products − reactants; ΔHc uses reactants − products.

practice.prompt: Explain why the ΔH calculated from average bond enthalpies differs from the experimental value.
checkpoints: Bond enthalpies are averages, not specific to these molecules
Calculation assumes all species are gases

practice.prompt: Use the equations below to find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g): C + O₂ → CO₂ ΔH = −394; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ ΔH = −283 kJ mol⁻¹.
Calculate ΔH for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ from ΔHc values (C₂H₄ −1411, H₂ −286, C₂H₆ −1561 kJ mol⁻¹).

paper1A.stem: Using bond enthalpies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹, what is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl?
Which equation represents ΔHf⦵ of water?
paper1A.why: One mole of product from elements in standard states.

paper1A.stem: A → B ΔH = +50; B → C ΔH = −80 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for C → A?
paper1A.why: A → C = −30, so the reverse is +30.

paper1A.stem: Which step in a Born–Haber cycle is always exothermic?
paper1A.why: Adding an electron to a Cl atom releases energy.

paper1B.data: Born–Haber data for MgO (kJ mol⁻¹): atomisation Mg +148; IE₁ +738; IE₂ +1451; ½O=O +249; EA₁(O) −141; EA₂(O) +753; ΔHf(MgO) −602.
paper1B.prompt: Calculate the lattice enthalpy of MgO and explain why EA₂ is positive.
paper1B.answer: Lattice = 148 + 738 + 1451 + 249 − 141 + 753 + 602 = +3800 kJ mol⁻¹ (booklet 3791). EA₂ is endothermic because an electron is being added to an already negative ion, which repels it.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Multiply bond or ΔHf values by the number of bonds/coefficients; check signs when reversing equations.
Use the v1.1 booklet values (e.g. C–H 414, C=O 804, O=O 498); older resources use different numbers.
Remember elements in standard states have ΔHf = 0.
When asked why bond-enthalpy answers differ, give both reasons: averages and gaseous state.
